build.section_title: Three kinds of projects. The same standard under the hood.
build.intro: What you see changes from one project to the next. What doesn't: well-structured data, payments checked on the server, tests that stop a bug before it goes live.
build.item1_text: Accounts, roles, subscriptions, dashboards. The tool that replaces your spreadsheets and manual follow-ups.
build.item2_text: Catalogue, Stripe payments, stock, orders, invoices. You sell; the system keeps the books.
build.item3_text: Fast, readable on mobile, well indexed. The front door, built with the same rigour as the rest.

method.section_title: Not one line of code without an approved plan.
method.intro1: An application rarely breaks where you're looking. It breaks in what you can't see: badly structured data, a payment nobody checked, a forgotten access rule. Those decisions are made at the start, or they get paid for later, at the price of a rebuild.
method.intro2: That is what scoping is for: putting the scope, the data, the security and the compliance in writing, before the first development quote. Optional for a marketing website, it becomes necessary as soon as there are user accounts, online payment or sensitive data.
method.e1_p1: Scoping is an architecture audit, carried out before any development estimate. In a video workshop, we start from how your business actually runs: what the application has to take payments for, protect or automate. Depending on the project, I draw from it the data model, the access rights, the payment flow, GDPR compliance and the scope of the first version, and hand them to you in a written report, delivered between 48 hours and 5 working days after the workshop. It is a preliminary engineering step, from {price} excl. VAT.
method.e1_p2: The report is yours. You can hand it to another developer: it is written to be carried out by anyone.
method.why_text: Because it is already the work. The data model, the access rights, the choice of payment provider: these are the decisions that cost the most to fix afterwards. A free quote guesses them. Scoping settles them, in writing.
method.demo_title: The interface shows. The architecture is decided.
method.demo_lead: , what your customer sees: a price, a stock level, a button.
method.demo_touch: Tap the button under the card.
method.demo_questions: Behind each element there is a question. Where does this price come from, and who checks it? What happens to the last item if two customers pay at the same time? What happens if the bank doesn't confirm the payment?
method.demo_p2: No mock-up answers these questions. They are settled during scoping, in writing, before the first development quote. That report is what you pay for: the decisions that keep the application standing, not one more pretty picture.

portfolio.section_title: Seven projects started. Six projects shipped.
portfolio.intro: Production-ready applications that run on their own — no hand-holding required. The list opens on the one still in private testing and closes on my very first build: the distance travelled is part of the shop window.
portfolio.project1_desc: A multi-vendor marketplace: every seller runs their own storefront and is paid into their own Stripe account, while the platform takes its cut at source and answers for the records — invoices, VAT, tax filings. A Next.js and NestJS monorepo, two languages, three subscription tiers.
portfolio.project1_build1: Taking money on someone else's behalf: the seller connects their own Stripe account, the funds never pass through the platform, and the commission is taken on the way past. No amount is taken on trust — totals are recomputed server-side from the database, never read from whatever the browser claims.
portfolio.project1_build2: Everything a payment sets in motion is written in one place, called identically by the Stripe webhook and by the net that sweeps through every fifteen minutes: a lost webhook, an outage longer than the retries, a session declaring itself complete and unpaid — the net queries Stripe the other way round and catches up without ever writing twice.
portfolio.project1_build3: Two buyers on the last item: the hold is placed in shared memory with a short lifetime, readjusted on every quantity change, then handed back to the database once the sale closes or the clock runs out. Availability updates for every connected buyer without anyone reloading the page.
portfolio.project1_build4: Running a platform means keeping other people's records: seller-to-buyer invoices and platform-to-seller invoices, unbroken numbering and frozen PDFs, VAT resolved live against the European register, tax reporting transaction by transaction, and an inventory ledger where an uninstrumented write breaks the test before it ever reaches production.
portfolio.project1_build5: The data-processing register is not written, it is generated by a command that reads the code: a hand-written document drifts from reality within three months. Same principle for retention — ten years for anything tied to a sale, two years for control actions, with the nightly purge logged in its own right.
portfolio.project1_build6: Interface copy lives in 92 files, one per screen and per language, assembled at build time. Eight tests forbid a file from sitting outside its index, a key from existing in one language and not the other, or an old monolithic file from reappearing beside the folder — it would win module resolution and silently mask the whole split.
portfolio.project1_challenge: Taking money on someone else's behalf changes every rule: the funds pass through, the liability stays. Hence a single payment path shared by the webhook and its safety net, stock held in shared memory and reconciled after every sale, and compliance treated as code — right of withdrawal, parental consent for minors, European obligations, VAT — rather than as a legal notices page.
portfolio.project1_stat_label: automated tests across 342 files, 61 of them full end-to-end journeys
portfolio.project1_stack: Next.js 16 · NestJS · PostgreSQL · Prisma · Stripe Connect · Redis
portfolio.project2_desc: A Mina and Ewe learning platform for the Togolese diaspora. Protected course materials, one-on-one sessions with a teacher, real-time messaging, subscriptions and a bookshop — in three languages, from the first screen down to the invoices.
portfolio.project2_build1: Two payment rails, one ledger: card payments in euros via Stripe, mobile money in CFA francs via CinetPay — order settlement is written once, server-side.
portfolio.project2_build2: Compliant invoicing: invoices and credit notes on two continuous numbering series, archived PDFs, whole-franc amounts on the CFA rail.
portfolio.project2_build3: Self-maintaining Cal.com booking: the webhook re-registers on every startup, a half-hourly sweep catches missed cancellations, a new teacher's room is created in one click.
portfolio.project2_build4: A complete transactional mail service in three languages, every time read on the recipient's clock — session reminders, subscription lifecycle, payments refused by the bank — with a send log in the database, purged after twelve months.
portfolio.project2_build5: Double opt-in newsletter: one Resend audience per language, one-click unsubscribe (RFC 8058), and a campaign trigger where you arm, then fire — a check first verifies the unsubscribe link is in the letter.
portfolio.project2_challenge: Two tills in two currencies had to produce a single set of books: order settlement is written once, server-side — and the CFA franc, which has no cents, forced whole-franc amounts all the way into the PDF invoices.
portfolio.project2_stat_label: automated tests against a real database, across 118 files
portfolio.project2_stack: Next.js 16 · NestJS · PostgreSQL · Prisma · Stripe · Socket.io
portfolio.project3_desc: A platform that runs a local farm co-op end to end: weekly baskets, members and producers, distribution shifts, treasury, PDF contracts and newsletters — live in production, built to be run by volunteers.
portfolio.project3_build1: Contract prices are never typed by hand: a single server-side pricing grid feeds the public form and the signed PDF contract alike, with a cheque breakdown exact to the cent.
portfolio.project3_build2: Treasury at paper pace: every cheque follows its cycle — in hand, at the bank, cashed or rejected — with a reminder to the member 30 days before deposit and a remittance list for the treasurer.
portfolio.project3_build3: Mail doesn't stop at sending: a Brevo webhook reports each message's actual fate, suppresses bouncing addresses and cuts the newsletter on a spam complaint.
portfolio.project3_build4: The weekly basket is generated from the seasonal catalogue, absent farms excluded from the draw, publication notified to active subscribers.
portfolio.project3_build5: Rich-text newsletters with batch sending, scheduling and drafts; a publication interrupted mid-send resumes on restart, without writing twice to addresses already served.
portfolio.project3_challenge: The real challenge wasn't technical: the tool is run by an association's volunteer board. Hence a built-in guide, screen by screen, and safeguards that refuse to start on an incomplete configuration rather than break down later.
portfolio.project3_stat_label: scheduled jobs running on their own
portfolio.project4_desc: End-to-end e-commerce for an Afro hair salon: a bilingual shop — the Love Your Curls line and jewellery —, Stripe payments, Brevo newsletters, and an admin space that holds it all, from orders to salon opening hours.
portfolio.project4_build1: No overselling possible: stock is checked before the Stripe session opens and decremented in a single atomic write — two customers can't buy the last item at the same time.
portfolio.project4_build2: Full or partial refunds from the admin: line items picked one by one, an immediate Stripe refund, a credit note generated on the spot with negative amounts, and an email to the customer.
portfolio.project4_build3: A built-in shipping chain: a CSV export ready for Colissimo Entreprise, and entering the tracking number marks the order shipped while sending the customer their tracking link.
portfolio.project4_build4: Abandoned carts don't freeze stock: a nightly sweep cancels orders unpaid for 24 hours and puts their items back on the shelf.
portfolio.project4_build5: A unified mail service: transactional emails on a shared base — email verification, welcome, order confirmation, shipping —, Tiptap newsletters through Brevo, and an HMAC-signed unsubscribe link: no unsubscribing someone else by tampering with the URL.
portfolio.project4_challenge: Two customers on the last item, a promo code redeemed twice at the same instant, two credit notes claiming the same number: every critical race was closed in the database — serializable transactions and conditional writes — rather than in the interface.
portfolio.project4_stat_label: before an abandoned cart returns its stock
portfolio.project5_desc: A community anime library, built solo: a catalogue imported from MyAnimeList, a six-status personal library, starred reviews, member submissions and an admin panel with moderation.
portfolio.project5_build1: Automated import from MyAnimeList via the Jikan API: the catalogue starts with 100 anime, an admin imports a pre-filled sheet in seconds, and DeepL translates synopses before they reach the database.
portfolio.project5_build2: Moderated contribution: any member can submit an anime — the entry waits in a moderation queue, pending, approved or rejected, before joining the catalogue.
portfolio.project5_build3: A six-status personal library with episode tracking: the progress bar advances, and an anime flips to "Finished" on its own when the last episode is marked.
portfolio.project5_build4: Layered security: differentiated rate limiting — free reads, limited writes —, honeypot anti-bot fields, IDOR protection: everyone edits only their own data.
portfolio.project5_build5: Accounts with email verification and one-hour reset tokens (Resend), user and admin roles, and an undeletable Super Admin.
portfolio.project5_challenge: Building a living catalogue on a third party's data: the Jikan import pre-fills, DeepL translates within a metered monthly quota, moderation filters — and if the translation key is missing, the site carries on in English rather than breaking.
portfolio.project5_stat_label: anime in the catalogue on day one
portfolio.project5_stack: Next.js 16 · Express · PostgreSQL · Prisma · Jikan API
portfolio.project6_desc: Showcasing a family estate nestled in the lush greenery of Montignac-Lascaux. For these three flower-named apartments, the goal was to craft a digital presence as warm as their gardens, ready to welcome travelers from all over the world.
portfolio.project6_build1: Five languages — French, English, Italian, Spanish, Dutch — with the choice persisted in the URL and the browser, for guests from all over Europe.
portfolio.project6_build2: No cookies, no trackers: GDPR compliance held by emptiness rather than by a banner — there is nothing to consent to.
portfolio.project6_build3: SEO built for a place: JSON-LD structured data, hreflang across five languages, a sitemap, and an llms.txt introducing the estate to AI crawlers.
portfolio.project6_build4: Apartment cards aligned with CSS subgrid, scroll-reveal animations via IntersectionObserver — no animation library.
portfolio.project6_challenge: Restraint as the brief: no back end, no cookie, no surplus framework — a five-language static site that loads fast and ages well, for owners with nothing to administer.
portfolio.project6_stat_label: languages, from the homepage to the legal pages
portfolio.project6_stack: React 19 · TypeScript · Vite · react-i18next · CSS Modules
portfolio.project7_desc: An artisan leather goods shop, and my very first build — kept here as it was. Stripe payments with webhooks, partial refunds detected automatically, PDF invoices, delivery tracking with an animated timeline: it is all already there, built while learning the trade.
portfolio.project7_build1: Already the foundations of the builds that followed: a signed Stripe webhook, stock validated server-side before payment, decremented after settlement and restored after a refund.
portfolio.project7_build2: Partial and full refunds detected by webhook, with stock restored and an email to the customer — the mechanism Fairy Chair Studio would later refine with credit notes.
portfolio.project7_build3: Dual-token sessions: a 15-minute access token, a 7-day refresh token with automatic rotation, and an anti-loop guard for requests expiring at the same moment.
portfolio.project7_build4: Delivery tracking across eight carriers: numbers validated by pattern, tracking URLs generated, shipping and delivery dates set automatically, an animated timeline client-side.
portfolio.project7_challenge: This is where I learned. The colours and the interface date from my beginnings, and I own them: the shop is no longer served, but the build stays in the catalogue, source open, as the starting point. The distance between that repository and Miabelangue is the whole journey this portfolio documents.
